prompt: What does `NULLIF(birth_year, '1900')` return for a row whose year is `1900`?
hint: The name says when it returns NULL.

choices.text: NULL
choices.why: Right. Equal to the second argument, so NULL; any other year passes through.
That is what it returns for a different value; for `1900` it returns NULL.
It never invents a zero; that would be `COALESCE` with a constant.

choices.text: An error
choices.why: Both arguments are text; it compares them quietly.

prompt: `COALESCE(discount, '0')` turns the website's blanks into zeros. What makes that safe here?
hint: A constant is a statement about meaning.

choices.text: Zero is the most common discount in the whole file
choices.why: Being common does not make it the meaning of a blank.

choices.text: `COALESCE` only replaces values it can prove are zero
choices.why: It replaces every NULL with whatever it is given; the proof is the analyst's.

choices.text: Lesson 2 showed the blank means no coupon
choices.why: Right. Without that evidence, the zero would be a guess.

choices.text: The website sends no coupons
choices.why: It does: the four coupon values appear on the website too.

prompt: The birth-year column had 338 blanks and 348 placeholders. How many missing years are there once the placeholders are blanked?
After dropping customers without a usable birth year, the shops' share of the customers falls from 25.5% to 8.4%. What does that mean for an average age?

choices.text: It is unbiased, since dropping never invents data
choices.why: Not inventing is true; unbiased needs the dropped rows to be like the kept ones.

choices.text: It is too small a sample to compute
choices.why: 1,601 customers is plenty for an average.

choices.text: It overstates the shops' customers
choices.why: The shops are under-represented now, not over.

choices.text: It describes mostly website and app customers
choices.why: Right. It is right for everyone only if the shops' customers are the same age.

prompt: Which practices make dropping rows more defensible? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Dropping per question with `dropna(subset=...)`
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Reporting how many rows the answer rests on
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Dropping every row with any blank, once, at the start
choices.why: That removes rows from questions that never needed the blank column.

choices.text: Comparing the mix of the rows before and after
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Why is zero the worst constant for the own fleet's missing delivery times?
hint: What is known about those deliveries?

choices.text: Zero is not a valid number of minutes for a delivery
choices.why: It is valid; it is wrong.

choices.text: They took 120 minutes or more; zero calls them instantaneous
choices.why: Right. The largest possible error per row, in the flattering direction.

choices.text: pandas refuses to fill a numeric column with zero
choices.why: `fillna(0)` ran without complaint.

choices.text: It moves the mean by only 1.7 minutes
choices.why: The small shift is why it looks harmless, not why it is bad.

prompt: For a category nobody recorded, what is the honest constant?
hint: It should say what is not known.

choices.text: The most frequent category in the column
choices.why: That inflates the biggest group with guesses.

choices.text: The category of the row above it in the file
choices.why: File order says nothing about a category.

choices.text: An empty string, so the column looks filled
choices.why: That hides the blank without explaining it.

choices.text: A word such as `unknown`
choices.why: Right. The row stays and the chart shows the gap.

prompt: Filling missing values with the column's mean leaves which statistic exactly where it was?

choices.text: The standard deviation
choices.why: It fell from 21.1 to 20.8.

choices.text: The share of late deliveries
choices.why: It fell from 10.5% to 10.2%.

choices.text: The mean
choices.why: Right; the spread shrinks and extremes are undercounted.

choices.text: The maximum
choices.why: The maximum is unchanged here too, but only because the mean is below it; it is not guaranteed.

prompt: Filled with the median, birth years keep the right mean and are wrong by 14.1 years per filled row. What follows?

choices.text: Imputation serves summaries, never the person in the row
choices.why: Right. A filled age in a customer's record is a fabrication.

choices.text: The median should be replaced by the mean in numeric columns
choices.why: The mean would err by about as much per row.

choices.text: A random draw would get each person right
choices.why: It was worse per row: 18.9 years.

choices.text: The truth file has errors in it
choices.why: It is the generator's own record; the errors are the fill's.

prompt: The true birth years have a standard deviation of 16.2; filled with the median, 13.3. By how many years did the fill shrink it?
Filling birth years by signup channel gave the same result as the overall median. Why?
hint: Group imputation works as well as the group predicts the value.

choices.text: pandas ignores `groupby` inside `fillna`
choices.why: `transform` gave each row its own group's median; they happen to be equal.

choices.text: Channel says nothing about age here
choices.why: Right; a group that does not predict the value cannot improve the guess.

choices.text: Every channel has the same number of customers
choices.why: They do not, and sizes would not matter anyway.

choices.text: The shops have no birth years at all
choices.why: Some shop customers do have a year.

prompt: Why can no imputation from the recorded delivery times fix the timer's blanks?
hint: What has a model of the recorded times never seen?

choices.text: There are too few blanks to fit any model to them
choices.why: A model is fitted on the recorded rows, of which there are thousands.

choices.text: Delivery times are not numbers
choices.why: They are minutes, the most numeric column here.

choices.text: Every blank lies above the longest time ever logged
choices.why: Right. Borrowing from the rows you have borrows from the wrong ones.

choices.text: The blanks are MCAR
choices.why: They are MNAR, which is why imputation fails.

prompt: Filling each blank several times, analysing each copy and combining the results is called ___ imputation.
Match each case to the right way to fill a day with no record.

A shop was open all day but its till crashed and recorded nothing. What should the day's sales be?

choices.text: Blank, and flagged as lost
choices.why: Right. Zero would claim no sales; the day is genuinely missing.

choices.text: Zero, since nothing was recorded that day
choices.why: Zero is right only when nothing happened.

choices.text: The day before's sales, carried forward
choices.why: Sales are a flow; yesterday says nothing about today.

choices.text: The average of the same weekday in the year
choices.why: A guess for a total, at best; written into the day's row, it is invented.

prompt: Why does flagging the own fleet's blanks give the late share exactly right?
hint: Every flagged delivery took at least how long?

choices.text: Flags are filled with the median of late deliveries
choices.why: A flag fills nothing.

choices.text: The truth file is used to set the flags
choices.why: The flags come from the blanks and what operations said, not from the truth file.

choices.text: Each flagged one is at least 120, so each is late
choices.why: Right. The bound answers the question with no guess.

choices.text: Flagged rows are dropped from the denominator
choices.why: They stay, counted as late.

prompt: Treating every flagged delivery as exactly 120 minutes gave a mean of 61.2. The real mean is 61.9. By how many minutes did the floor fall short?
What does a flag give the next person that a column filled with medians does not?

choices.text: A smaller file that loads faster in every later tool
choices.why: A flag adds a column.

choices.text: Which values are guesses, so a better method fits in later
choices.why: Right. A filled column looks complete and hides its guesses.

choices.text: A faster query
choices.why: Speed is not the point.

choices.text: A complete column with no blanks left in it for anybody to handle
choices.why: The blanks stay; that is the point.

prompt: Why does Ana write the decisions as a view over the raw table instead of updating it?
hint: What happens to the raw rows?

choices.text: Views run faster than tables because they are cached
choices.why: A view runs its query each time; speed is not the reason.

choices.why: It does not.

choices.text: A view hides the flags from other analysts

choices.text: Raw rows stay intact; queries read the decisions
